speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: SANCTIONS AGAINST ITALY NEWS BROADCAST FROM STATION 2RO ROME, ON WEDNESDAY, JUNE 17
speechtext:
Yesterday my right hon, friend, the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) referred to a news 'broadcast from Rome on the evening of Wednesday, June 17, which stated that the Canadian council of ministers at a meeting held the previous day, that is June 16, had decided to favour the abolition of sanctions. I replied that I would make inquiry as far as possible to see if there was any ground for believing that this statement indicated knowledge in advance of the policy of the government announced in the House of Commons on June 18. I do not think it does.
The statement quoted is incorrect since as a matter of fact the question was not discussed in council at all on June 16 as stated. The general position had been discussed some days earlier, and council's decision reached at the time, but the final wording of the statement of the government's position was taken up at the special meeting of council on the morning of June 17. I notice in the Montreal Star of June 16 the following disipatch from Ottawa:
It is understood that the government is giving consideration to-day to its position in respect to sanctions against Italy. What precisely will be the attitude is not officially determined. It is believed, however, that the government is practically certain to join that section of British thought which favours the lifting of the penalties.... Discussion is tentatively fixed for Thursday. The Prime Minister on that occasion is expected to define the attitude towards a continuance of sanctions. Inasmuch as these penalties in time of active war did not frustrate the annexation of Ethiopia by Italy, their continuance, in time of peace, may be regarded as futile.
I think there is little doubt that the statement to which my right hon. friend referred was simply a more positive expression of the above, or similar anticipations. For some days before the announcement of the United Kingdom government the press contained similar surmises as to the decision which would be announced.
I may repeat that there is not the slightest indication that the decision of the government was communicated to any outside person.

The other day a return was brought down in regard to questions I had asked with respect to the names of those who had been invited to attend the unveiling of the Vimy war memorial. My question this morning is to ask the Prime Minister whether it is his intention to attend that ceremony?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
In reply to my hon.
friend I may say I should like very much to be able to be present at the ceremony at Vimy next month, particularly because of the nature of the ceremony and also in view of the fact that His Majesty the King has accepted the invitation of his Canadian ministers to be present, and the president of the French republic has accepted the invitation of the government of Canada to be present on the occasion. I have however had to ask myself what may be involved in the way of absence overseas during the next twelve months, and as hon. members know, the coronation ceremonies will take place in London in May of next year, to be followed by an imperial conference, and I expect, unless something unforeseen happens, to be present in Great Britain at that time. I had anticipated that it might not be necessary for any reason other than in connection with the unveiling ceremony at Vimy to visit Europe this year; I am inclined, however, to believe that the importance of the meeting of the League of Nations Assembly which is to be held in September, and which will have to do with the critical situation in Europe and the revision of the

Foreign Policy-Mr. Woodsworth
covenant and which may mark a fresh start in the affairs of the League is so important that it would be desirable for the leader of the government of Canada to be one of the representatives of the government at Geneva at that time. In these circumstances I fear I may have to forego what would be an exceptional privilege, namely, being present in France at the unveiling of the monument at Vimy. I have asked my colleagues the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) and the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Power) to represent the government at the Vimy ceremony, and it has been so arranged.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO PROBABLE DATE OF OPENING OF NEXT SESSION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this would seem to be the appropriate place to ask the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) if he has any information to give the chamber regarding the probable date of the opening of the next session of parliament. I quite appreciate the difficulty to which he has referred with respect to his own personal *movements, but I recall that on more than one occasion he made similar inquiries of the late administration, and it occurred to me that this might be a suitable occasion on which to indicate generally his intention. I agree that if the League of Nations is to revise the covenant this year it is highly desirable that the Prime Minister of Canada should be present. Whether or not that would interfere with any plan which might be prepared for the early opening of a session of parliament of course I do not know. But it is quite clear that the right hon. gentleman would have to be absent moderately early in 1937, and it is probable that we would not have parliament continuing to sit in his absence. This is a matter of some interest to hon. members, and I have been asked to try to ascertain whether the government has any information to communi-[DOT] cate in this regard.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I address a few words to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) before you leave the chair. Hellas intimated that he may attend the meeting, of the league at Geneva. I am sure the house will be delighted to learn that he has made that decision. It seems to me the world situation is important enough to necessitate the attendance of the Prime Minister, but may I point out that he has not given the house a clear statement of the policies he will advocate at Geneva. I recognize that if there is to be a reorganization of the league there has to be a good deal of latitude allowed, because the whole subject would be one of negotiation. At the same time, since the issues of peace and war are so largely dependent upon what is done at Geneva, it seems to me only right that the Prime Minister should give us, even now, some indication as to the general lines he intends to advocate at Geneva.
Further than that, in this session the opportunities for the debating of international affairs have been obviously very unsatisfactory.. Last night the hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Miss Macphail) intimated that she had been very anxious to present her views in the matter. She had not been able to do so earlier in the session. Near the last of the session we were promised that we would be given a day to debate the subject, although

at an earlier stage that opportunity was refused us. The "day" we were promised dwindled down to two hours.
Last night we had the curious spectacle of the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) attempting in the midst of considerable disorder to present a highly technical and learned dissertation on some of the constitutional issues involved in the action of the government with regard to Geneva. It was impossible for any of us to give careful attention to his presentation. That is an absurd situation. The only opportunity we have to discuss a matter of such great importance is in the dying hours of a session. I would ask the Prime Minister whether or not he could give us the assurance now that near the beginning of the next session a *committee may be appointed charged with the definite responsibility of studying Canada's foreign policy. I cannot see where there could be any objection. None of us is anxious to drag to the light of day matters which ought to be kept quiet. We recognize clearly that certain things may come to the knowledge of our Department of External Affairs which could not at all times be made public, but surely we must get away from anything like secret diplomacy. More than that, it seems to me very desirable that the public at large should take an interest in its external affairs. It was all very well when Canada was a colony for us to confine our attentions to matters within our own boundaries; but to-day Canada is part of a big outside world. I believe it is the responsibility of this house to debate these matters, and that of the government to afford opportunities for wider discussions leading to greater public interests. I offer this suggestion to the Prime Minister.
I have one further suggestion along another line. No person could sit in the house last night and fail to be impressed with the ridiculous situation which results when we try to pass a great variety of estimates at the last moment. Indeed, I have often thought that the present method of handling estimates in committee of the whole is not the best that could be devised. Last night in connection with a particular estimate the minister in charge quite naturally did not know exactly the details in connection therewith. He had to wait until his deputy was called in. All along the deputies must attend in the house, and there is the curious spectacle of the minister leaning over to get a few sacred words from his deputy in order that he may pass on the information to the house.

Sacred, or
salient?
{Mr. Wermenlinger.]

"Sacred" is the
word I used, and perhaps in this connection it is as good as "salient." We as members of the house are supposed to remain in our places to hear wide discussions covering the whole range of government departmental administration. It is obvious that a good many of us are interested in only one department, and can be interested in only a few departments; certainly we cannot all be interested in the whole wide range of subjects covered by all the departments.
Some of us have earlier advocated a change of procedure. It might be possible, just as we have experimented a little with a special committee on national railways, to have the estimates referred to appropriate committees. The fisheries committee could deal with the fisheries estimates; the agriculture committee with the agriculture estimates; the external relations committee, if one can be set up, could deal with external relations. In such a committee we could call in the deputy ministers who could be questioned in the easier and less formal atmosphere of a small committee. If necessary we could even call in outside witnesses who might give expert evidence. The members would be able to specialize in certain departments, and that specialization carried on year after year would give a great deal of added interest to the lives of a great many members who are keenly interested in specific affairs and in certain details but who are not so much interested in the general debates in the house.
Someone may say, "Well, but that would not give all the members an opportunity to speak." It would, because the report would come from the committee, and if there were any outstanding evils or any questions of importance we still would have the opportunity to discuss them in the house. We would not be precluded from doing that. Of course it may be said that Hansard would not get it all. From my standpoint I think that would be a decided advantage. It would shorten the session tremendously if we did not have Hansard record all the casual observations made during the discussion of the estimates. I venture, therefore, to ask the Prime Minister whether he will not at least consider some change in procedure by which the estimates may be placed for consideration before appropriate committees, thus saving an enormous amount of the time of this house, as well as adding to the efficiency of parliament.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in reply to my hon. friend, first with respect to his desire

Estimates-Mr. Mackenzie King
that I should make a clear statement as to the government's policies on matters pertaining to the League of Nations and the European situation, which I presume would be the most important feature of all, may I say that I think I made a very full, very complete and very clear statement to this house as recently as Thursday of last week. From what I have since seen of the press comments on the statement then made it would appear that the journalists of the country at least had the same impression. I confess that at the moment I cannot think of anything further that could be said with advantage. What will have to be considered at Geneva in September will depend very largely upon what appears on the agenda of the League of Nations at that time. As my hon. friend and members of the house generally know, the assembly of the league meets again on the thirtieth of this month to resume .the session which was adjourned last fall. After that session is held the government will be in a better position to know what questions will be uppermost at the meeting of the assembly in September. Until that session is concluded I do not think there is anything I can add to the statement which was given to the house the other night. I feel, however, that my hon. friend and other members of this house may with some degree of confidence rest assured, that the position which will be taken by myself and the colleagues who may be present with me at the assembly will be one which will very much accord with the views of this house. As far as I am able to sense the situation I believe members of all parties in this house are pretty well united with respect to the views they entertain on Canada's foreign relations. There may be differences here and there, but as a Canadian people I think we are singularly united in the essential features of our foreign policy, and certainly those essential features will be kept to the fore at the meeting in September.
My hon. friend has spoken of the desirability of having a committee to study foreign relations. May I say that there is nothing to preclude any number of members of the House of Commons forming themselves into a study group for any purpose at any time. In Great Britain that is done in connection with many matters in the House of Commons, and I see no reason why those who are interested in foreign affairs should not constitute themselves at any time into a committee for the purpose of making as complete and thorough a study of foreign relations questions as can be made. I would point out, however, that we have a standing committee of this house which deals with industrial and international relations. That would appear to be
an appropriate committee to consider, as far as one of the standing committees might consider, matters relating to Canada's foreign policy.

But may I point out, without any desire to interrupt that in practice that or any committee can consider only such matters as are referred to it. As far as my memory goes, the only matter ever referred to that committee with regard to foreign affairs was a motion of my hon. friend from Grey-Bruce (Miss Macphail) some years ago.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
What my hon. friend has just said only emphasizes what I am saying. The hon. member for Grey-Bruce evidently suggested that some question should be referred for study to the committee and the suggestion was acted upon. If hon. members have suggestions to make as to particular subjects to be referred to that committee I think there is every reason to expect that their suggestions would be favourably considered and the necessary references made if it were apparent that the desire to have them so referred was at all general.
However, the matter of procedure is quite secondary to the importance of having subjects themselves carefully considered, and I must say that I entirely agree with my hon. friend as to the desirability of having the fullest study given .these all-important questions. Probably the more study that is given to them the less will be the desire for premature discussion in many phases. With regard to discussion I am one of those who believe in the wisdom of the fullest possible discussion except where it is perfectly obvious that such discussion in this house and this country may have the effect of adding to the difficulties of those who are contending with very great problems in other parts of the world. I must say that, with the knowledge the government has had of the very critical nature of the European situation this year, I make no apology to any hon. member of this house for having done my utmost to prevent premature discussion of questions that were inflaming the minds and the passions of peoples in the old lands. I think we owed that much to them, to see that nothing should be done here in the way of adding fuel to what I believe was very near to becoming a pretty serious conflagration across the ocean.
With respect to the procedure to be adopted in connection with the discussion of estimates, what my hon. friend has suggested has been discussed on previous occasions. There is much to commend his suggestion, but at this
Privilege-Mr. Bennett

stage of the session I should not like to say more than that between now and next session I will ask my colleagues to consider with me the wisdom of adopting a course such as my hon. friend has suggested. Perhaps when parliament reassembles, if hon. members feel it their desire so to do, we might have a discussion of the matter on the floor of the house. In regard to the estimates and the time of bringing in supply, may I say that this year the main estimates were laid on the table of the house during the very first week of the session, so the house has had the supply before it for a long time. If we have not concluded with the supply I would say it has been because we have had an exceptionally heavy and important sessional program with a great deal of legislation embodied in bills on one subject and another, which was relatively of much greater importance than anything which appears in the supply. In the estimates we have sought to avoid as far as we could items that we believed might prove to be contentious. In this first session of parliament we have not only endeavoured to get through but have actually succeeded in having enacted legislation which in other parliaments would have occupied the time and attention of this house over two or three sessions instead of being brought as has been the case with this year's program within the compass of a single session.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before you leave the chair might be a .proper opportunity to mention a matter of privilege. The other evening the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) stated that the house had been compelled to spend fifty-two per cent of its time in sitting and listening to the leader of the opposition. I hope his other remarks were nearer the truth than that. The fact is that not twenty-five per cent of the percentage stated by the Minister of Agriculture was taken up by the leader of the opposition.
I desire to point out that I occupy a statutory position and am paid the salary of a cabinet minister. During this session, except for the time when I was indisposed, I have been here continuously six hours a day, from three to six o'clock and from eight to eleven o'clock except for two days. It may well be that I have had a good deal to say, but I can assure the house that the Minister of Agriculture was not present during all that time to hear me, because his duties, kept him elsewhere for a considerable part of the time. I
have a duty to perform and I have endeavoured to perform it. I have been continuous and assiduous in my attendance in this house because I conceived it to be my duty to do so as long as I occupy the position I do.

I want to quote a typical letter I received the other day:
I think the government is doing wrong by cutting down on the fishery patrol. I think it would be better to cut down on the office staff and increase the fishery patrol. There are a number been fishing and selling blue back salmon for the past two weeks-
And that is illegal.
-and they get away with it. At Powell River you can buy fish all the year round both in season and out of season. What is really essential is the conservation of fish; clean out all the streams that the salmon go up to spawn and find a market for the fish.
On one occasion a number of men got together and proposed to the government that if they would appoint a man to round up offenders against the regulations they would supply a man who would do the work for nothing-and men do not generally work for the government for nothing. Obe man wrote me to this effect: "The main thing is that the Vancouver office will have no strings on our man." Do you get the idea? If the government would send out an independent man, someone not directly interested in the department, the cost of the Vancouver office could be cut in half and that would provide a good deal of money for ground officers, because the permanent man is paid by the year while the ground officers are paid only six weeks or three months.
In this connection may I quote the leader of the opposition. The other day we were discussing the estimates of a department, and while the right hon. gentleman was not criticizing, he used this language:
The department is an efficient department and I think it reflects great credit upon the deputy head, but I think if you said to him, "Go and cut down that staff by twenty-five per cent," he would do so and have a more efficient organization than he has to-day.
And he was not contradicted. The Minister of Railways the other day, giving the reasons for the amalgamation of the various branches of his department, said that there was a central purchasing office in one branch, with a staff of twelve, in another a staff of five, in another four, and so on. Then the leader of the opposition made the statement that in his time they cut out 12,000 officials, and he said:
That is a terrible thing to say, and yet the service was more efficient by reason of it.
And he added that that was a still more terrible thing to say. He went on to warn

the minister that even, if he found that some of the superfluous staff had to be paid he should nht keep them in the office but if necessary' pay them to keep them away from the office, because the organization would be improved by having a smaller and more practical staff.
Coming to the'question of hatcheries, I believe that in British Columbia some ten are closed out of sixteen or fourteen; yet the cost of overhead has been cut down only two per cent. It is notorious that there must be a good deal of work in overhead connected with the running of the hatcheries, and yet the cost has been reduced only two per cent, whereas some of the praetical works have been cut down seventy-five per cent. What do we want with a purchasing agent and a statistician in the Vancouver office? The minister may reply that there are no 6uch officials. That may be true; but I was a member of the house when they were appointed in 1928-29 and I know what they were called then. I protested against them at that time; I said we did not need men filling those positions. Now they are called something else, but they are still there drawing salaries. Then we have an inspector of chartered boats. We might as well have a chaplain; indeed he would do more good. These boats are chartered by the government, but the government takes no responsibility. If the boat is unseaworthy, if there is anything wrong with the engine, that is up to tie owner; the government will not even be responsible for insuring it. The owner must insure it himself. All that is necessary is to see to it that the boat is reasonably seaworthy, the engine capable of running; and the inspectors who travel on boats under their own control can readily discern anything wrong with them. But we have a man whose ostensible business is to inspect these boats.
Unfortunately there is an idea abroad that any official with a high salary and a fancy title is bound to produce results, but that is not so. A Welsh rabbit, which is neither Welsh or rabbit, sounds nice, and I compare the two, because in the case of the Welsh rabbit the element is ennobled by a fancy name and some skill in cooking, while in the other case an ordinary clerk is dignified by a fancy title and a high salary. But the fundamental basis in both is the same-just a plain ordinary piece of cheese, useful and wholesome, but just-cheese. A gentleman who was once appointed for the first time to the position of minister was struck by the enormous number of officials in his department, and he conceived the brilliant idea of

Supply-Fisheries
making inquiries, not of his de&ity, who would say at once that there were not nearly sufficient officials, but of the officials themselves. He sent a circular to them inquiring of each official what his or her duties were. One official exlaimed, "What a shameful thing to ask us to do. What do I do anyhow?" Many years ago a certain man was elected as alderman in a certain city and,'being one of those pestiferous fellows who ask a lot of questions, he fixed upon two employees and demanded to know what they were doing. This was in February when there was four inches of snow on the ground, and by steady persistence he elicited, against the opposition of the officials, that these two men had been put on in the previous June to make hay in the park, and they were still making hay in February. In this house I was once approached by a man who asked me to help him in connection with his superannuation. In the course of conversation he said, "After all, the government have not treated me too badly, because my job petered out four years ago and they have only fired me now." That is an illustration of how things go on.
Tell us the whole story.

It is good to put these departments now and again through the threshing mill and separate the wheat from the chaff. They are honeycombed with dry rot in some cases, and bureaucratic and departmental politics. An official in one of the departments once told me: "I have been here a long time; I have not suffered myself, but I have seen more harm done to the public service of Canada by the exercise of departmental politics than ever any of you political chaps could exercise, because you have a nemesis waiting for you in the House of Commons; you can be exposed, but departmental politics is subtle and underhand and you don't know what is going on." I was very much struck the other day by the remarks of the leader of the opposition when the Minister of Marine was introducing the bill in connection with the harbour board. He complimented the minister for doing it right away, and he said, "If you had not done it then, you never would have done it," and he instanced his own experience where he had the same desire to do it and was not able to; and I think the Minister of Marine knows now that if he had not done it when he first went in he never would have done it at all. This is a parallel case. The Minister of Marine was taking control of a thousand men; this is a much smaller thing and could
be very much more easily done. I do beg the minister to put his hand to the cleansing of the Augean stable; I know it would be a great boost to his reputation. We need a great shake up, different views, and different policies.
Let me quote an illustration. I will not take the trouble to look up the page, but in the last fishery report the chief supervisor of fisheries for British Columbia said that the pack of salmon was "very satisfactory"; he said it had amounted to 1,582,000-odd cases. But the record year a few years before that was 2,000,000-odd cases. That is a drop of practically half a million cases, equivalent to three or four million dollars, a heavy drop, about twenty-five per cent, but he said-it is "very satisfactory." Well, there is the official point of view. It is "very satisfactory" that we have dropped our output twenty-five per cent. What are our competitors doing? Here is the record of Japan. A few years ago she was not in the picture. Last year she put up 2,418,000 cases, nearly a million cases more than we did; say, at $5 a case, 85,000,000 more than our total output. But the official says everything is "very satisfactory." Is it?
Then take Newfoundland. A complete reorganization of Newfoundland fisheries is provided for by the newly appointed fisheries board. Yes, they are taking time by the forelock and doing what is necessary to a complete reorganization. That is what we want in British Columbia, but the answer is, "very satisfactory." Is it? "Now" is the watchword of the wise; now is the time; now is the accepted day, as it is said. If the minister would cut loose from these palsied influences of the past he would have an opportunity to create a reputation and a record for himself that have not been attained by any minister for many years past, because we have never had for any length of time a separate minister of fisheries, although for a few months the Hon. E. N. Rhodes was a very efficient minister. But now the present minister is making a new start and he has got a chance to make a record for himself that may do wonderful things for the industry and for his own reputation. He can cut down on the overhead, and, as the leader of the opposition says, with better efficiency-not with less efficiency but with more; that is the point. Let him spend the money he saves in that way on patrol men, on guardians, on air patrols, on the destruction of sea lions and hair seals, on the building of fish ladders to let the fish get up where sometimes now they cannot for lack of water; on the cleaning
Supply-Fisheries

of creeks to help natural spawning. If these things are done the fishermen will have their livelihood assured, and that is about all they want. All they need after that is a market. If the minister would take out of the $300,000 vote sufficient money to help with the freight charges, they would have a market. The British Columbia government, I understand from Victoria the other day, has expressed no desire to take up the $50,000 out of that grant, so that that $50,000 will rest with the department and I suggest that this would be the most profitable use to make of it. Let me quote this one sentence from an editorial in a fishery paper published in British Columbia:
Fishermen realize that the best aid given them is the guarantee of an assured future and the maintenance of a source of income which, if allowed to go to ruin, no appropriation, least of all to "needy fishermen," will be able to reestablish.
That is the spirit of our men out there. They do not want pork barrel aid. They want to be helped to help themselves, and they will be only too glad to do their share.
One more thing I suggest, and it is all important. Make the Fisherman's Loan Act workable. Was not a question answered the other day that not one loan had been granted under it? Certainly not, because the regulations are such that loans cannot be made, and never will be except to a very small extent. Make the act workable, and then there will be a chance for these men to help themselves. The British people are doing it. I have a record here showing that they are going into a scheme of this kind. Now the minister has got this $50,000 that is available, so to speak, that should be credited to British Columbia out of that $300,000, I suggest that it should be used to help the causes I have indicated and make the Fisherman's Loan Act workable. By "workable" I mean, conditions by which they can take advantage of it. Make it apply to sums greater than a thousand dollars if necessary, and make it apply to the boat and gear. It is now confined to the man who has got real estate which, forsooth, he must occupy. How can a fisherman be occupying real estate? But he has to occupy it and it has to be worth double the amount granted. Take the halibut man with a boat worth $25,000; he may not have enough land to put a henhouse on, but for that reason he cannot get any loan. If the act were made workable in that way it would be a tremendous advantage.
I put forward these views without any desire unduly to criticize the minister. I have not criticized the minister; he is only new at

the thing, but I am pointing out conditions as I see them and have seen them for a long time. I claim to have some knowledge there. I have lived in a fishery district for over forty years, and for nineteen of those years I have represented it either in the house at Victoria or here, so I may claim to have some working knowledge of conditions. I should appreciate it if the minister would investigate the matters along the lines that I have indicated.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. E. MICHAUD (Minister of Fisheries):
speechtext:
Just a word in respect of
the remarks that have been, placed1 before this committee by the hon. member (Mr. Neill). I am pleased to be able to inform him that, with the additional amount provided in the supplementary estimates, it will be possible this year to have expended for patrol work the same amount that was expended last year, and have the same patrol and the same force that we had last year. There is the amount as requested in the main estimates this year, in item 145. With the amount provided in the supplementaries, added to the amount which we are asking the house to vote in the first column, we shall have exactly the same amount that was expended last year-not that was voted by parliament, but that was expended for the service of patrol that my hon. friend has pointed out.
Item 145?
Yes. With the additional amount provided for in the supplementary estimates we shall have enough money to give to British Columbia the same amount of patrol work that the government did last year.

H the minister will allow
me, the decrease is $141,548, vote 145.
That is the whole vote.

No, that is vote No. 145.
It is decreased $141,548 and increased $40,000 by the supplementaries.

But last year of that
vote $913,702 was actually spent. This year we are asking parliament to vote $878,600 plus $40,000, which will make almost $5,000 more than was actually expended last year. That is why I say I shall be able after this vote goes through to implement the recommendation made by the hon. gentleman as well as other hon. members representing fishing districts, and give the patrol that was provided for last year.
My hon. friend has complained about the Vancouver office, about there being too many cooks, too many officials. Unfortunately I

Supply-Fisheries
am not familiar with the local situation there, but I promise my hon. friend that as soon as it is possible for me to do so I shall have this investigated and see for myself what the conditions are, and if they are as represented I can assure him that not only fifty per cent but seventydive per cent or one hundred per cent if necessary will be dismissed if they are superfluous. Of course there are some officials whose work may not appear to be necessary, but when one considers that in British Columbia during the year we have twenty-one boats belonging to the government, two large boats and nineteen smaller ones, and besides that during the summer we hire on an average eighty-two boats for patrol work, the amount of work involved is apparent. There is an official there, I understand, whose duty it is to supervise that fleet of small craft, direct them and see that they are in working order. But if the work of that man after investigation is found to be unnecessary I can assure my hon. friend that his services will be dispensed with.
My hon. friend made one remark which I think was not justified. He said that the books or accounts of that department were kept in a disgraceful manner. If that be so this department is not responsible for it, because the books and accounts are kept ,by the treasury department. They have officials of their own keeping the books and accounts of our department as well as of other departments, and the officials of the Department of Fisheries are not responsible.

If the minister will allow
me, perhaps I should not have said that the books are kept in a disgraceful way; I should have said that the system is such that it is almost impossible to ascertain what was spent on this or that.

Well, the criticism should be directed to the Department of Finance, which has jurisdiction over the treasury department. However, this matter I am sure will be taken note of by those responsible.
As to departmental politics, I am safe in saying that I know nothing about it, and I have had no actual fact pointed out to me. But if any hon. member has a complaint to make about political activities by officials of the department I shall be pleased to have the facts laid before me, and if after inquiry the official is found guilty of breach of his duties the minister will not countenance any such activities on the part of any official.

Even at this late hour in the session I desire to say a word. We are
now dealing with the main fisheries estimates, on which we would naturally discuss both matters of policy and matters of routine. I hope the presentation of that vote at this late hour in the session is not an indication that the fishing industry is not considered of paramount importance in this committee and to this country. Coming as I do from a county which is largely interested in the fishing industry I regard it as my duty, as far as I am able, to place before the committee and the government the importance of the fisheries.
Fisheries are of national importance, anc have an international aspect. While the fisheries department has direct control of the fisheries I regard our fisheries as an industry with which practically every department of the government is concerned. I know of no man who could do more for the fisheries than the Minister of Trade and Commerce, by making proper trade arrangements with other countries whereby we should be able to sell our products and bring new money into this country. The fisheries invite foreign trade. For that reason I trust that the Minister of Trade and Commerce during the recess, in conjunction with the Minister of Fisheries, will give his attention to the matter of marketing our fish products in foreign countries.
The same is true of the Minister of Transport. Transportation is a big item in connection with fish. It is a bulky product, freight rates are high, and transportation is all important. The Minister of Transport can give great assistance to the Department of Fisheries in facilitating transportation, both as to cost and as to speed, and making fish more readily available to people throughout Canada and to the people of other countries. The Minister of Agriculture also, through the acts relating to cold storage and farm loans, in which the fishermen are interested, can do his part. So that while the fishery estimates have to do principally with the regulation of the fisheries, all these departments are represented in the picture. The fish trade is unique and important and should appeal to the imagination of every member of the government.
Fisheries are of greatest importance to us in the maritime provinces. We are a maritime people. If we are to prosper as a part of Canada it must be in the industries that are naturally ours; I refer to activities on the sea-the fisheries and the mercantile marine. If we build up the industry that is naturally ours, when we get it to a state of efficiency and secure the trade it will be ours
Supply-Fisheries

against competition and will be economically sound. For that reason I say that as far as the maritime provinces are concerned, while we have our interest in farming and other industries, common to other provinces also, if we want to excel as a port of Canada it must be in our activities upon the sea. That has been our history in the past. There was a time when we had more ships per capita upon the ocean than any country in the world. Our men sailed to every port on the seven seas. Our fisheries sustained us and were the admiration of foreign countries. In fact one of the reasons set out for the pact of confederation was that this country would develop the fisheries of the maritime provinces.
We hope that the minister who has now taken charge of the fisheries of Canada will amplify these thoughts and see to it that this natural primary industry of the maritime provinces receives every consideration. The main countries with which we are in competition are stimulating their industry, and we must put ourselves in a position to compete. Geographically we are in a favoured position; Nova Scotia and the maritimes are adjacent to the finest fishing banks in the world. There is no good reason why we should not meet competition of every kind. This is one thing which will help to relieve unemployment in my constituency. I therefore enlist the sympathies of the Minister of Labour, because he too must be interested in the fisheries. Fishermen are a class who can live on a smaller amount of this world's goods than can most people, and they deserve consideration.
Something has been said about cutting down the fisheries estimates. The votes for fisheries are very low, and perhaps they have been pared down lower than is justified. But we must realize that we have supplementary estimates which to a certain degree make up the loss.
I notice that the wages of guardians have been lowered, and I must say there is some justification for that action. In the rural parts of Canada I believe it is a mistake to have government men getting more money than people engaged in private industry. The man who works for a private company should not be placed in the position where he must envy the government employee. Everybody is looking for a government job, because it is paying more than anybody else. I believe hon. members will agree that the reduction per day of wages of these men is in some degree justified, because it shows a disposition on the part of the government to save money

-for other active items of fisheries estimates. If we are serious in our efforts to save it in the Department of Fisheries I am sure the fishermen will cooperate as far as possible. At any rate the total expenditure this year will be greatly increased.
The last government made provision for loans to fishermen who offered real estate as security. The principle of offering loans is a step in the right direction, but it was inadequate for the purposes of the fishermen because, as 'a rule, they hold no real estate. I suggest that the legislation should be amplified so that the fisherman may get a loan on his gear or boats. The proper way to do that would be to give the loans through the people who know how to give them, and know what credit should be given. I suggest that the government could make some arrangement with the chartered banks, branches of which are found in every fishing village. If the government would guarantee or share the guarantee of the loans the fisherman could get the small amount of money he required, because he usually does not need very much.
The Minister of Finance might look into the matter during the recess in an effort to reestablish the fisherman. I believe with a proper expenditure of money and proper attention our fisheries will stand the strain and stress of days to come.

Item agreed to.
Building fishways and clearing rivers, $1,400.

I suggest the amount in this vote is unreasonable, to the last degree. Last year there was a vote of S6,000, and this year it is only $1,400. I can point to one island alone where we could use all that. I know the minister has arranged for a further sum of $3,000 in the supplementary estimates, but when we are shutting up the hatcheries we must surely give further help in building fishways and clearing rivers. The total amount will be only $4,400 as against $6,000 for last year, and I suggest that instead of a decrease there should have been an increase towards helping to preserve the fish. There is a general idea that the best way to help them is by clearing rivers and building fishways. I realize the minister has obtained a substantial increase, but to begin with he suffered a cut which was out of all reason. My quarrel perhaps should be with the Minister of Finance; possibly the Minister of Fisheries did not present sufficient of what we call in the west a "skookum tumtum," or a strong mind, that is he did not take a sufficiently firm stand with the Minister of Finance.

Supply-Fisheries
Mr. IvINLEY: May I say that if hon. members want the thrill of their lives they should come to Nova Scotia and catch a tuna. In that way we would enlist the interest of the tourist department in the fisheries of Nova Scotia.
And if you want good salmon, come to the Fraser river.

Item agreed to.
Fish culture, $240,000.

This is an expenditure for fish culture and, I assume, includes hatcheries. The cut is no more than two per cent. Could not the minister have made a greater cut in this vote, in view of the reduced expenses in connection with hatcheries?

It is a fact that the closing of the sockeye hatcheries in British Columbia will bring about a saving of about $50,000, but I wish to repeat-if I did not make it clear yesterday-that only the sockeye hatcheries are being closed. All other hatcheries in the rest of the country are maintained. Further I must add that they are not closed because it was found that artificial propagation was not proper or adequate, but because it was found the natural propagation of sockeye salmon was sufficient to meet the requirements. The money we saved by closing those hatcheries is being expended on other hatcheries throughout the country-in British Columbia as well as in the rest of Canada. We have estimated that out of the $50,000 we will spend $43,500 to improve other hatcheries.
After the minister closes what he is going to close in British Columbia, are there not only four left? He is going to close ten of them.
We are closing Anderson lake, Babine lake, Smiths Falls, Kennedy lake, Lakelse lake, Pemberton, Pitt lake, Rivers Inlet and Harrison lake.
That is nine; you are keeping four.
We are keeping Cowichan lake, Argenteuil, Lloyd's creek, Nelson, Penask and Summerland.

Those are merely sport
fisheries. They are little better than breeding ponds, in some cases. I cannot see where we can save $50,000 out of certain hatcheries, and then spend all of it on these small hatcheries.
No, on the rest of the country.
The minister said something about a fifty thousand dollar reduction in the amount to the fish hatcheries in British Columbia. Would he give us the reduced vote to British Columbia?

It is not a separate vote for British Columbia; it covers all the hatcheries in the country. Fish culture was taken under one vote. We have closed some of the hatcheries in British Columbia; the closing of the hatcheries I have just enumerated will cause a saving of $50,000, but the money is to be expended for the improvement of some hatcheries in British Columbia and others in the rest of the country.
I take it that the minister proposes to reduce the vote to British Columbia by fifty per cent, and to distribute it in other parts of the country.
No.
Well, that is the only place hatcheries are being eliminated.
No; it is because British Columbia is the only place where there are sockeye hatcheries.

No; yesterday I spoke about the building of a new hatchery in Nova Scotia last fall. Can the minister explain why, when the government had in view a change in policy, it should build a new hatchery? What was the cost of it, and where was it built?

I am told that the hatchery in Nova Scotia was constructed to carry on the artificial propagation of Atlantic salmon in order to maintain the supply, while the report of the biological board is to the effect that on, the Pacific coast, in connection with sockeye salmon, natural propagation is sufficient to maintain the supply.

I can hardly agree with that; if you look up the report of the biological board they do not say that. What they do say is this: they have decided that while propagation by artificial means can be done, the results are not sufficiently more profitable than the natural propagation to make it desirable to continue that, but certainly they do not say that the natural system is sufficient in British Columbia, because the facts are against that. We are going down every year, a thousand cases this year and perhaps a million cases next year. I cannot quite grasp why, in view of the information gained by the biological board, it should be necessary to start a new station on the Atlantic at a considerable expenditure. One would think the conditions
Supply-Fisheries

on the two coasts were practically similar. Was there some depletion of a run on some particular river that justified this expenditure, or what was the idea?
I am told that it was in order to build up the Atlantic salmon fisheries in the eastern part of Nova Scotia.
What particular rivers were concerned?
I am told that practically all the rivers in the eastern part of Nova Scotia were concerned.
And what was the cost of the hatchery?
And for that we had to go hungry in British Columbia.
Oh, no.

Officials were discharged from the hatcheries in my district in the fall of the year, when there was work for them to do. When I inquired as to the reason I was told that the vote had petered out. I inquired further, and I have a letter from the deputy minister saying that the construction of a new hatchery in Nova Scotia took up a good deal of their money.

I do not think it is fair to draw the conclusion that the hatcheries in British Columbia were closed in order to provide money for the construction of a hatchery in Nova Scotia. There was no relation between the two.

The minister misunderstood me; that was not what I was trying to convey. I did not say the hatcheries were closed, but in the fall of the year, when the hatcheries in British Columbia were still running, their work was hampered. Men were taken off, and when I asked why I was told there was no more money. If you put a man in a hatchery to do the work of two men, provided he was not underworked before, the assumption is that the work will suffer.

I understand that in the fall of last year the appropriation was practically exhausted, and the work in the hatcheries all over Canada was curtailed to the limit in order to make the vote extend to the 31st March.
Let us be frank about it; was it in order to help the political fortunes of Mr. Ernst?

I do not know anything about that.
IMr. Neill.]

I cannot agree with my hon. friend from Comox-Alberni with regard to the appropriation for the hatchery in Nova Scotia. I think that salmon hatchery is destined to do a very good work with regard to the rivers in eastern Nova Scotia.

Item agreed to.
Marine Biological Board of Canada, $188,300.

What is the extra $13,000
for in the supplementaries?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We will come to the
supplementaries in. a moment.

I notice that the total
vote for this board, including the item in the supplementaries, is $201,000. Would the minister explain whether this covers salaries and expenses and, in case an investigation is carried on. such as was carried on at Cultus lake, whether any money comes out of the fish culture vote to assist in that work?
Yes.

Would the minister give
me the details of the salaries and expenses?

The salaries at Nanaimo station are as follows:	Doctor Clemens,
$5,400; Doctor Foerster, $3,900; C. R. Elsey, $2,760; Doctor J. L. Hart, $3,000; C. Mc-Mottley, $2,400; Doctor A. L. Pritchard, $2,760; A. L. Tester, $1,620; J. P. Tully, $1,740; W. E. Ricker, $1,800; Miss D. Dickinson, $960; Miss E. Robinson, $960; Miss E. Keighley, $1,020 and T. Russell, $1,200. Then there is the foreman at Cultus lake, W. F. Baxter, $1,500; E. L. Kennedy, $1,200, G. G. Thomson, $1,200. J. H. Stannard, foreman, Queen Charlotte Islands, $1,500, and D. Crocker, $1200.
I am not so much interested1 in that. The information I wanted was whether this vote for the biological board, totalling $201,000, is for salaries only.

Yes, for salaries and
investigations all over the country.

No expenses connected
with it? Are the expenses paid out of the fish culture vote?

There is the cost of
publicity and the travellling expenses, and there is the salary of Doctor Huntsman, as well as the salary of Miss Rigby, who is assistant editor and clerk. There are ex-, penses totalling about $18,000, but this covers salaries for the Prince Rupert station, the Halifax station, the Nanaimo station and the St. Andrews station.

Supply-Fisheries

I just wish to point out
that the vote for fish culture, which has been condemned by some, amounts to $240,000. That has to do with one of our main industries, perhaps the best of all the industries having to do with fish, the sockeye salmon industry. To-day, on the other,hand, we are paying $201,100 in order to maintain this board of scientists. Once' more I wish to stress the importance of the minister taking into consideration the application of a little more practical knowledge and consultation with some of the practical men engaged in this industry, instead of leaving it all to a board of scientists.

I asked the reason for the
$13,000 that appears in the supplementary estimates.

That	provides $10,000
for a biological station in the lower St. Lawrence and $3,000 to pay the salary of a lobster investigator in the maritime provinces. The lobster supply is getting low and for some years the lobster fishermen and the lobster packers have been requesting that a scientist should be entrusted with the duty of investigating the cause of his diminution of supply.

There are one or two general observations that I wish to make. The matter to which I shall refer may be new to the minister, but it certainly is not new to the department. For a number of years the fishermen in Nova Scotia have been agitated over the continued use of the beam trawler. Several royal commissions have been appointed to consider this matter and have made reports adverse to the continued use of the trawlers.

Did the hon. member say
that all those reports were unanimous?

I did
not use the word "unanimous" at all.
What did you say?

I said
that the reports were against the use of the beam trawlers.
All the reports?

All of
them.
That is not quite correct.

I know
some of the reports were not unanimous, but in my training a report of the majority is the report. I was going on to say that what
might be termed a makeshift policy was adopted some years ago for the licensing of these trawlers, and I understand some licences have been issued this year. Before a licence is issued the department must be satisfied from evidence that the issuing of a licence is necessary in the interests of the trade. My idea of evidence is that an opportunity is given to both sides to be heard, and my complaint is that on this occasion only one side was heard. I am going to suggest to the minister, on behalf of the fishermen whom I represent, and I know I can speak for the fishermen in many other counties, that no licence should be issued until both sides to the controversy have been heard.
I am sorry I must differ with the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Kinley); I do not believe sufficient money is appropriated for the purpose of properly guarding our streams. One of the best assets that the province of Nova Scotia could have from the tourist standpoint is streams well stocked with sport fish. I do not know where the hon. member got the idea that the salaries paid to these guardians were too large. The hon. member's idea was that they were so large as to be almost discriminatory when compared with other industries. These guardians are paid only $25 or $30 per month.
Not in my county.

I have
the figures under my hand. They are employed for only two or three months and I do not think you can expect to have an efficient guardian when you pay such low wages. If you want to have your streams properly protected you must pay more money for this service. I cannot recall the term used by the hon. member for Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neill), but whatever it was I hope the minister will remember it in his attitude toward the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) in the coming year when estimates are being considered.

Mr. Chairman, I think
my hon. friend must have misinterpreted what I said. In one stream in my county we put on more guardians, but the department is paying them less. I think that is sound business. I am not saying that our streams should not be properly guarded; on the contrary what I say is that it is better to have more guardians, and that can be done at the lower rate; the same money employs more guardians.
I should like to say a word about the use of 'beam trawlers. In the light of conditions that exist I cannot see how anyone in authority
Supply-Fisheries

in this country can think that the beam trawler is necessary at the present time for the success of the fisheries. Some years ago the Maclean commission was appointed to report on conditions in the maritime provinces and they reported against the use of the beam trawler. Doctor Cyrus Macmillan was perhaps the strongest member of that commission advocating abolition, and he became Minister of Marine and Fisheries later on. He is now a professor at McGill university. It is true that Judge Maclean, for whose opinion I have a high regard, had a different opinion from that of his colleagues, but that difference was quite small. In effect he said that the beam trawler should be used only for the purpose of taking up the slack, to use the vernacular of the fishermen; he said that it should be used only when necessary to provide a continuity of supply.
The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cardin), who was then Minister of Marine and Fisheries, presented an order in council to the government, which he said had been prepared with the assistance and on the opinion of his deputy. The government passed that order in council, which in effect, entirely prohibited the use of the beam trawler. This order in council was questioned and it became the subject of litigation in the courts. After an adverse opinion had been rendered by one court, an appeal was started, which was later withdrawn. The tax was paid back to the one firm that had paid it.
Another order in council was passed by the government of the right hon. gentleman to my left which set out in effect that beam trawling would be permitted only if it did not interfere adversely with the line fishermen, and that before a licence would be issued the minister must be convinced that they would not decrease their purchases from the line fishermen. In the face of this order I have received resolutions from groups of fifty, one hundred or two hundred fishermen in my county who have been laid off by these same companies and who have since been unable to get any work. I contend that if there ever was a time when the provisions of that order in council should be enforced, it is the present.
Then we had the Jones commission which investigated the economic conditions of the province of Nova Scotia. That commission reported, recommending that the beam trawler be gradually abolished. They pointed out that it was not necessary. I am not giving my own opinion. My opinion is the opinion of the fishermen whom I represent, and they are unanimously against the 'beam trawler, but

that is not the opinion I am giving now. I am quoting the opinion of scientific men who heard the evidence. The Minister of Public Works himself travelled along the coast taking the views of fishermen from place to place. The beam trawler people themselves say it is not essential to the carrying on of the industry.
This matter was before the price spreads committee at the last session and that committee reported against the beam trawler. With one exception, Mr. Young of Weyburn, the committee was unanimously in favour of the report against the beam trawlers. Mr. Young was in favour of the trawlere but all the others reported absolutely against them, and in the course of the evidence given before the committee the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens), who was then chairman, made a comment which I should like to read. I quote:
By the Chairman:
Q. Just before you leave that, may I say this:	your idea is that an international
arrangement be made to discontinue the use of those trawlers?
A. Surely that would be the logical thing to do, for there is not any necessity for beam trawlers to have continuity of supply; and they are a great expense to the companies who are operating them. They admit that themselves very frankly. I know the president of the National Fish Company, Mr. Britton, and that particular year I was here on the subject of advertising, and he admitted to me that the only reason they wanted beam trawlers was that it gave them a certain amount of independence.
In other words, they want the beam trawler as a club to hold over the fishermen. Not a great amount of fish can be caught by the trawlers. There are three trawlers and it is estimated that each can catch nine million pounds of fish a year, or twenty-seven million pounds. Personally, I think that is an exaggeration, but those are the figures. Now that is a large part of the deep sea catch in Nova Scotia. We may be told that they do not catch a large percentage, but the fact is that it puts the beam trawler corporation man in the position where he is a primary producer and he can say to the fishermen, "I have a beam trawler coming in to-morrow; you take what I give you for your fish or you can go home." The fisherman has no bargaining power.
We are not opposed to the beam trawler as an economic factor; we are not opposed to progress. But it is not real progress, for the fishermen can produce better fish more cheaply than the trawler can. And what is more, the fishermen do not destroy fish. At this moment the United States government is concerned about haddock fishing on the banks

Supply-Fisheries
adjacent to Nova Scotia, and there is a suggestion that beam trawlers be prohibited west of St. Pierre. The banks off the coast of Nova Scotia are being ruined by the beam trawler. However, that is an international matter with which we are not concerned at the moment. The point is that we want the Canadian market for Canadian fishermen, and we think that they should have some way of determining the price for which they must sell their product. But the beam trawler is one instrument that defeats that object. We may have to come to a minimum price for the fishermen. To my mind the fishermen of Canada, whether they are right or wrong, will never be satisfied until the beam brawler is abolished. We have a population of only 10,000,000 while in the United States there is a large market with a population of 120,000,000. If we had a population of 20,000,000, the beam trawler might be necessary, but we have a condition that does not exist in any other country. Ground fishing is only one part of the activities of our fishermen; they must fish in the outports to catch lobster, mackerel, herring and seasonal fish that come along the shore. Put these men in Halifax and make them coal heavers and beam trawler operators and you will denude the shores of Nova Scotia and ruin the industry. The government must know, surely, that scientific men like those who composed the commissions that have studied this matter are not men who would be parochial in their opinions or who would give opinions without reason. And the opinions are there.
I submit that in the interests of employment the experiment should be tried and if necessary the beam trawler operators could be compensated. Just allow them the profit they showed in their income tax returns last year. This is a matter that has been before the country a long time and we will keep it before the country, not because we are opposed to progress but because we believe that progress should be genuine, and the interests of our men who need work should be paramount. There is no other means by which men can live than by working, and until you can allow men to sit at the table without working you must see to it that they have work.

My hon. friend from Cape Breton North-Victoria and my hon. friend from Queens-Lunenburg seem to be under the impression that the Minister of Pisheries has the power to abolish the beam trawler. I have not, nor did I have that power last spring when the time came for the renewal of licences. It is true eminent men have given their opinion as to the necessity of the steam 12739-263
trawler, but one fact remains, and it is this. The parliament of Canada has dealt with the question in all these investigations that have been carried on, and in 1929, I believe, passed section 56 of the Fisheries Act. Under the provisions of that act power was given to the governor in council to make regulations for the operation of steam trawlers. These regulations were questioned before the courts and one tribunal decided that they were ultra vires inasmuch as they were prohibitive in effect.
The trawlers were taxed by order in council.

The tax was so high that it was prohibitive; it really prohibited the trawler from operating. If parliament wanted to prohibit the trawlers it would have passed a statute forbidding the use of them; but it provided for the regulation of these trawlers. So far the regulations have been made and administered by the Department of Fisheries; and I felt last spring, when the time came for renewing licences, that, not having the power to refuse to issue licences, I should confine myself to renewing those that had been in force in the previous year or for the last few years.

The minister is no doubt aware that so far as the companies carrying on the fishing business in the maritimes are concerned, it is a matter of privilege, because there is only one company that is allowed to have steam trawlers.
If they complied with the regulations and made application in due form I renewed the licences. Last year one application was refused because the conditions had not been complied with.

That was in my constituency and I compliment the minister on not having granted it. The minister takes the point that the statute was for regulations, but I want to point out to the minister that the order in council was in effect a prohibition-absolutely-which showed the intent of the government of that day.

Item agreed to.

This is the item dealing with civil government at Ottawa. I have prepared elaborate data that I proposed to unload, but I am going to take mercy on my weary fellow members and cut it down very substantially.
Hear, hear.
Hand it over.

I will put it into three minutes if I can. First, I just wanted to correct a misstatement that was made when I was speaking on this matter on March 3. I was reported somewhat generally in the press as having said that in my opinion the civil servants of Canada were asleep. That was a mistake. What I said was, certain sections, and that I am prepared to stand up to. To say it applied' to them all would be doing a gross injustice to the civil service, a large majority of *whom are very faithful, conscientious people, and some of them entirely devoted to their work. I then intended to deal with, though now I am only going to summarize it, some of the statements the deputy minister put into the mouth of his minister in connection with the figures, with which he dealt with the utmost abandon. Discrepancies of twenty-five per cent and in some cases seventy per cent I can readily prove. I proposed to show also the type of figures that his chief supervisor in Vancouver sent out, but I showed it to the minister, so I will not repeat it. It was not a case of typographical error; it was a straight case of faking figures, they faked figures at the bottom in order to make them agree. That was at the least gross carelessness. If the minister wants details I have them under my hand. Page 56.
Intentional?
Absolutely. If it is not intentional the man is a fool. It is not a typographical error. I will show it to the minister if he wishes.
I have seen it.

The reason I say it is intentional is this. They add up seven columns and they do not add them up correctly, but to make them agree with the other two totals they put in a false statement. You have only to look at the thing, on page 55. If you take the number of cases inspected of sockeye, 270,000, and reject 21,000, you surely do not have 349,000 left, do you? It does not need a statistician or a purchasing

agent to tell you that. But they make the totals correct. Then I show that the deputy minister's own bulletin, the bulletin for May, says that the British Columbia product increased $550,000 last year, but if you compare it with his own report on page 6 you will find the increase is only $452,000, a trifling difference of $98,000. But here are the only points I want to make. I am taking their own figures. They show that the marketed value for 1935 went up $550,000 while the landed value to the fishermen, according to the January bulletin, went down $178,150, showing that the fishermen got less for their product that year while the cannery men got a large increase. That goes to support my contention, and that is the trend of my remarks, that the policies of the departmental officials and their sympathies in British Columbia lie wholly with the big cannery interests, as the men who are prominent in the business world, in the financial world, in the social world, and perchance in the political world also. Their sympathies go there; they are not with the working fishermen.

The sympathy of the
minister goes with the working fishermen.

I thank the minister for his
kind words, and I shall look forward with hopeful anticipation to his making good on that.
I see in the item there is a purchasing agent in the office at Ottawa. What do we want a purchasing agent for? In the same building there is a purchasing agent for the Marine department; on the same floor or the next one there is a purchasing agent for the Public Works department. There is also a government contract supervising committee that takes charge of the salvaged stuff that has to be disposed of. What does that department need a purchasing agent for? Will the minister tell us why? It will tax his ingenuity, I think.

It is to purchase all that the department needs. Most, though not all, the purchases for the eastern section of the fisheries department are made in Ottawa through tender from the main office. It is only in British Columbia that we have a special purchasing agent, a man in Vancouver who looks after the purchases in British Columbia, but all the purchases in the eastern section are made in the head office at Ottawa through that gentleman.
In that case, what does he buy?

All kinds of things.

Supply-Finance
Stationery? Coal? Gas?

No. We have boats on the Atlantic. He buys supplies for all the boats, and supplies for all the hatcheries. There are repairs needed for our boats, and everything is done through tender. I think the officer justifies his existence as such by the work that under my observation he has to do. Possibly a concentration of all the purchasing departments of the government might result in some saving, but it is a matter of policy.
Could we not cut out the man in British Columbia? The Atlantic purchasing is done here; could not the Pacific coast purchasing be done here also?

I doubt it. The purchasing of supplies for British Columbia would be difficult to do from Ottawa. The distances are against us; it is so far away that it takes a long time to communicate. I understand the system that now prevails in Vancouver has been in vogue for over twenty years. Prior to that time the department was administered wholly from Ottawa, and it was not found satisfactory. That is the information I have.

We have a three day mail service now; try air mail and telegraph and wireless; I do not think the distance has got any greater. Is it not a fact that within the last five or six years the department in British Columbia bought three boats? I forget the names of them all, but one, I think, is called the Vanidis. If my information is not erroneous they have already had to rebuild two of them, or they have rebuilt one and contemplate rebuilding the other two. I do not know whether "rebuilding" or "reorganization" is the correct word, but I understand some very big alterations have had to be made on a comparatively new boat.
I understand some alterations were made in a boat.
A new boat.
A new boat which was bought some years ago.
Then for God's sake get a new purchasing agent.

Item agreed to.

I should like to say one word with respect to this matter. I mentioned it to the Prime Minister when we rose. I refer to the question of the payment of sessional stenographers. During the last regime there were no statutory increases, and it will * be recalled there was a reduction in payments made to civil servants. The policy which had been adopted for many years in connection with the sessional stenographic staff was a salary of $4 per day to begin with; when they had served a second session they went to S4.50 and in the third session they went to S5. But after the failure to provide statutory increases, and the diminution of salaries which took place in consequence of a general reduction in the salaries of civil servants, that was not continued. It has resulted in some ill feeling, if I may use so strong a word, on the part of those who have served in some cases three and four sessions, and in other cases longer than that. Mr. Speaker will no doubt be aware of the circumstances. The old rule of the sliding scale has been discontinued. I remember having personally discussed the matter at the instance of those then in charge, and with the gentleman who looks after the staff. He told me-and I believe it is still so-that beginning with a fixed rate and increasing fifty cents the next year and fifty cents the following year was eminently and entirely satisfactory. I trust when the committee on internal economy makes a final adjustment of these matters at the end of this session they will return to the old rule departed from by the late government at the time I have indicated, when there was a lessening of salaries paid to civil servants and when statutory increases were discontinued.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think I can only explain it by reciting the facts of the case. As I think my right hon. friend knows, there are certain provisions of the Returned Soldiers' Insurance Act under which the Minister of Finance has to give a decision with respect to the disposition of the insurance. In this case-I suppose I can mention the name, since it appears in the item in any event- the assured under the Returned Soldiers' Insurance Act named his first wife, Maggie Amanda Roper, as beneficiary. He obtained a divorce in the United States, if my memory serves me aright, and remarried. Both the assured and his first wife were advised by officers then administering the act that the second marriage could not be recognized and that the first wife must remain as the beneficiary of the insurance. The first wife, therefore, continued to pay the premiums and did so until the death of the assured. Later, however, the pension commission recognized the divorce, and therefore the first wife is ineligible to receive any benefits.
When the matter came before me I thought it was very unjust that the first wife, on the basis of an assurance given years ago by responsible officers, should continue to pay
